source.title: Apollo: An Exploration of Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models
source.authors: Orr Zohar; Xiao-Han Wang; Yann Dubois; Nikhil Mehta; Tong Xiao; Philippe Hansen-Estruch; Li-Cheng Yu; Xiao-Fang Wang; Felix Juefei-Xu; Ning Zhang; S. Yeung-Levy; Xide Xia

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws but does not test power-law pretraining loss, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocations, or the other listed claim versions. Its own Scaling Consistency experiments measure correlations in downstream video-benchmark accuracy across model sizes, a different result.
record.gate_note: The paper reports accuracy correlations for design variations across LMM sizes, not held-out cross-entropy loss curves or compute-optimal parameter/token splits. These accuracy-correlation results are recorded as findings that fit no listed version; citations to other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper only discusses traditional scaling laws, as background and as something it relaxes. It fits no loss curve, no compute-optimal split and no downstream-vs-scale law. Its Scaling Consistency results are R2 correlations of design-variation video-benchmark accuracy between fine-tuned LMMs built on different LLM sizes. That is a different construct: transfer of design rankings, not how loss or performance scales. Tables 14–15 show higher average accuracy at larger LLM sizes, but the paper fits no predictive relation to them. The models mix Qwen1.5 and Qwen2 families and are fine-tuned rather than pretrained from scratch, so this does not test V6 or V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that design decisions made on moderately sized LMMs (~2–4B) trained on ~500K samples transfer reliably to larger models, even across model families ('Scaling Consistency'). They present this as a cheaper alternative to scaling-law studies. The rest of the paper concerns video-LMM design findings and the Apollo models.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates accuracy correlations for LMM design choices rather than reproducing the original loss-scaling measurement or compute-optimal fitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported accuracy correlation varies with model-size pair; the paper identifies stronger transfer around 2–4B than at smaller sizes. For the 4B-to-larger-model comparison, correlation plateaus around ∼500K samples; smaller models show less consistent behavior across dataset sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: R2 of design-variation average accuracy between LLM sizes: 0.938 for 4B vs 7B, 0.694 for 0.5B vs 7B. The correlation to 7B rises roughly log-linearly with the smaller model's size (Fig. 3, fitted y≈0.1·log(x)+0.78). For the 4B model it plateaus near 500K training samples. Appendix D extrapolates R2 of about 0.86 to 32B and 0.84 to 72B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Design-choice rankings for fine-tuned video LMMs transfer across LLM sizes once the smaller model is about 2–4B, and the transfer correlation grows log-linearly with model size.

record.problems: The results concern downstream video-benchmark accuracy correlations rather than pretraining loss or loss-law fits. The scaling-consistency experiment uses four stated language-model sizes, and the authors note that broader applicability to larger sizes needs further investigation. The dataset-size correlation is described qualitatively rather than reported as numeric values at each size.

untested.parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss in parameters, tokens or compute; no loss curves are reported.
Extrapolating loss from small runs to much larger runs.
Effect of depth, width or shape on loss at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in video or multimodal training. The paper cites prior LMM scaling-law work but fits no power law.
Predictable downstream improvement with scale or loss. Raw accuracies rise with LLM size (Tabs. 14–15), but only four sizes from mixed families are used and no scaling fit is made.
Dependence of exponents or optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to no version. The states 'observed' describe the scaling-consistency finding itself, not any claim version. The Appendix D extrapolation of R2 to 32B/72B is the authors' projection, not a measured result.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Predicting larger-run held-out loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Architecture-shape effects on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in video or other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss; cross-size correlations of design-variation accuracies are not this test.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and bending of loss curves.
